newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Conventional Swiss view of WWII record changing.
newsitem.headline: Conventional Swiss view of WWII record changing.

text.p: Tough public scrutiny of Switzerland's dealings with Nazi Germany during World War Two has changed conventional views of its wartime history, according to a new survey.

The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology's military department found 60 percent of Swiss now believe the country avoided involvement in the war mainly as the result of its financial and business dealings with the Nazis.
This compares with a 1983 poll in which 61 percent said they believed Swiss military preparedness was the main factor that kept Switzerland out of the war.

The new poll of 1,014 people, conducted in March 1997 and published in Thursday's Neue Zuercher Zeitung, showed only 31 percent of people aged 18 to 29 and just 28 percent of those with higher education held the traditional view.

It also said that a relatively high percentage of "I don't know" responses from respondents under 30, those over 60, from women and from the better educated illustrated the considerable uncertainty surrounding the historical question.

Sociologist Kar Haltiner, who did the survey, concluded that belief in the traditional interpretation -- the military kept the Swiss out of the war -- stemmed from above-average trust in the army coupled with below-average trust in the media.
The view that Switzerland was spared because of its commercial ties to the Nazis reflected declining trust in authorities, especially the Swiss parliament, the article said.

Debate about neutral Switzerland's wartime role is raging domestically and abroad. Switzerland's defenders say the tiny country had no choice but to trade with surrounding Axis powers, while critics say it shirked its moral duty.
